questions.q: What does a web cache deception (WCD) attack trick a web cache into doing?
choices: Storing sensitive, dynamic content that the attacker can then retrieve
Injecting attacker-controlled content into responses served to other users
Deleting all cached static resources to force a denial of service
Revealing the origin server's private TLS key
questions.explain: WCD tricks a cache into storing sensitive, dynamic content (such as another user's data). The attacker then requests the same URL and is served the victim's cached response.

questions.q: What is the root cause that makes web cache deception possible?
choices: The cache server and origin server handle or parse the same request differently
The cache always ignores Cache-Control headers
Browsers encode all special characters before sending requests
The origin server never sets cache keys
questions.explain: WCD exploits discrepancies in how the cache and the origin interpret a request. The cache treats an ambiguous request as a cacheable static resource while the origin returns dynamic, sensitive content.

questions.q: How does web cache deception differ from web cache poisoning?
choices: Deception gets private content stored so the attacker can read it; poisoning manipulates cache keys to inject malicious content served to others
Deception injects malicious content served to others; poisoning reads private content
They are two names for the exact same attack
Deception targets browsers while poisoning targets DNS resolvers
questions.explain: Poisoning manipulates cache keys to inject malicious content into a response served to other users. Deception exploits cache rules to get private content stored, which the attacker then retrieves.

questions.q: In the WCD attack flow, what happens after the victim's browser makes an ambiguous request for sensitive content?
choices: The cache treats it as a static resource and stores the response, which the attacker later requests
The origin blocks the request and alerts the victim
The browser caches the response locally and never contacts the server again
The attacker's session cookie is automatically sent to the origin
questions.explain: The cache treats the ambiguous request as a request for a static resource and stores the response. The attacker then requests the same URL and receives the victim's cached response.

questions.q: What is a cache miss?
choices: No stored copy exists, so the request goes to the origin and the cache decides whether to store the response
A stored copy is served directly without contacting the origin
The origin refuses to answer the request
The cache key fails validation and the request is dropped
questions.explain: On a cache miss there is no stored copy, so the request is forwarded to the origin. The response passes back through the cache, which uses its rules to decide whether to store it. A cache hit is when a stored copy is served directly.

questions.q: A cache key is usually generated from which two parts of the request (name both)?
questions.explain: Cache keys are typically built from the URL path plus query parameters (and can also include headers, content type, etc.). Requests with a matching key are treated as equivalent, so the cached response is served.

questions.q: Which of the following are types of cache rules based on strings in the URL path that WCD exploits?
choices: Static file extension rules (e.g. .css, .js)
Static directory rules matching a path prefix (e.g. /static, /assets)
File name rules matching exact names (e.g. robots.txt, favicon.ico)
Rules based on the client's TCP source port
questions.explain: WCD exploits cache rules keyed on the URL path: static file extension rules, static directory (prefix) rules, and exact file name rules. TCP source port is not a cache rule type described here.

questions.q: When looking for a target endpoint, which HTTP methods should you focus on, since state-changing requests generally aren't cached?
choices: GET
HEAD
OPTIONS
DELETE
questions.explain: Focus on GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS. Requests that change server state (like POST or DELETE) are generally not cached.

questions.q: Why should you inspect raw responses in Burp when hunting for a sensitive target endpoint?
choices: Some sensitive data isn't visible on the rendered page but appears in the raw response
Burp automatically decrypts the database for you
The rendered page always hides the cache headers
Raw responses bypass the origin's authentication
questions.explain: Some dynamic, sensitive data is present in the raw response even though it isn't visible on the rendered page, so checking raw responses helps you find a worthwhile target.

questions.q: Why does each test request need a cache buster (a different cache key)?
choices: Otherwise you receive a stale cached response instead of a fresh one from the origin
It encrypts the request so the WAF cannot read it
It forces the origin to use a different database
It disables the victim's session cookie
questions.explain: Without a unique cache key per request you may get a stale cached response. A common method is to add a query string and change it on each request; Param Miner can add a dynamic cachebuster automatically.

questions.q: After crafting the malicious URL and letting the victim's response be cached, why fetch the same URL in Burp rather than the browser?
choices: Apps may redirect sessionless users or invalidate local data in the browser, which could hide the vulnerability
Burp caches responses more aggressively than a browser
Browsers cannot send GET requests
The origin only answers requests that come from Burp
questions.explain: Fetching in Burp avoids browser behaviors (redirecting sessionless users, invalidating local data) that could mask the cached sensitive response.

questions.q: What does an X-Cache value of 'hit' indicate?
choices: The response was served from the cache
The response was generated dynamically by the origin
The cached content was outdated and had to be revalidated
The response was not found in the cache and came from the origin
questions.explain: X-Cache: hit means the response was served from the cache. 'miss' means it was fetched from the origin, 'dynamic' means the origin generated it dynamically, and 'refresh' means outdated cached content was revalidated.

questions.q: True or false: a response with Cache-Control: public and max-age greater than 0 proves the response is being cached.
questions.explain: It only suggests the response is cacheable; it does not prove it, because the cache may override the header. Confirm with headers like X-Cache and by comparing response times.

questions.q: Static file extension rules such as .css and .js are described as what in most CDNs?
choices: The default caching behavior
A feature that must be custom-written for each site
Disabled unless a WAF is present
Only available on the origin, never the CDN
questions.explain: Extension rules (.css, .js, etc.) are the default in most CDNs, so the goal is a request for dynamic content carrying a static extension that the origin ignores but the cache sees.

questions.q: For the URL /user/123/profile/wcd.css against a REST-style origin with a traditional-style cache that has a .css rule, what happens?
choices: The origin ignores wcd.css and returns the profile; the cache treats wcd.css as a .css file and stores the profile
The origin returns the wcd.css stylesheet and the cache ignores it
Both the origin and cache return a 404 error
The browser blocks the request before it reaches the cache
questions.explain: A REST origin maps /user/123/profile to an endpoint and ignores the extra wcd.css segment, returning the profile. A traditional-style cache sees a file wcd.css and, with a .css rule, caches the profile response.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of a path-mapping WCD attack?
choices: It works only on the specific endpoint tested, since abstraction rules differ per endpoint
It works on every endpoint of the whole server at once
It only works over HTTP, never HTTPS
It requires the victim to be logged out
questions.explain: Path-mapping discrepancies are specific to the endpoint, because URL-to-resource abstraction rules differ per endpoint. Delimiter attacks, by contrast, tend to work across many endpoints.

questions.q: With the payload /profile;foo.css against a Java Spring origin, how do the origin and cache differ?
choices: Spring truncates at the ; (matrix variable) to /profile; most caches see the full path ending .css and cache it
Spring reads the full .css path; the cache truncates at the ;
Both treat ; as the end of the path
Neither side accepts the ; character
questions.explain: Spring uses ; for matrix variables, truncating to /profile. Most caches see the full /profile;foo.css path ending in .css and, with a .css rule, cache the dynamic profile.

questions.q: On a Ruby on Rails origin, why does /profile.ico return the profile while /profile.css causes an error?
choices: .ico isn't a recognized format so Rails uses the default HTML formatter; .css is recognized but has no CSS formatter, causing an error
.ico is a recognized image format that returns a favicon; .css returns a stylesheet
Rails blocks all requests ending in an extension
Rails caches .css itself but refuses .ico
questions.explain: Rails uses . to select a response format. .css is recognized but has no CSS formatter (error), while .ico is unrecognized, so the default HTML formatter returns the profile. A cache with a .ico rule then stores it.

questions.q: For /profile%23wcd.css (%23 is #), what discrepancy makes this cacheable?
choices: The origin decodes %23 to # and truncates to /profile; the cache does not decode %23, sees .css, and caches it
The cache decodes %23 and truncates; the origin sees the full path
Both sides decode %23 identically, so there is no discrepancy
The browser strips %23 before the request is sent
questions.explain: A delimiter-decoding discrepancy: the origin decodes %23 to # and truncates to /profile, but the cache doesn't decode %23, so it sees /profile%23wcd.css and its .css rule caches the response.

questions.q: True or false: because delimiters are generally consistent across a server, a delimiter-based WCD attack often works on many endpoints.
questions.explain: Delimiters tend to be consistent server-wide, so a working delimiter attack often applies to many endpoints, unlike path-mapping attacks which are endpoint-specific.

questions.q: When brute-forcing delimiter characters with Burp Intruder, what setting must you change?
choices: Turn off payload encoding so the delimiter characters aren't URL-encoded
Turn on payload encoding so every character is escaped
Set the attack type to cluster bomb
Enable the built-in cache buster in Repeater
questions.explain: Payload encoding must be turned off (Payloads side panel > Payload encoding) so the candidate delimiter characters are sent raw rather than URL-encoded.

questions.q: Static directory cache rules match what part of the URL?
choices: A path prefix such as /static, /assets, /scripts, or /images
The file extension at the end of the path
The exact full file name
The query string parameters
questions.explain: Directory rules match a path prefix (e.g. /static, /assets). Exploiting them relies on path-traversal basics to make the cache and origin disagree about the real path.

questions.q: What is URL path normalization in this context?
choices: Converting path variants to a standard form, e.g. decoding characters and resolving dot-segments
Encrypting the path so caches cannot read it
Removing the query string from every request
Mapping a REST endpoint to a file on disk
questions.explain: Normalization converts URL path variants to a standard form, such as decoding encoded characters and resolving dot-segments (../). Parsers vary a lot in how they normalize, which creates exploitable discrepancies.

questions.q: Why must the dot-segments in a traversal payload be encoded (e.g. ..%2f instead of ../)?
choices: Otherwise the victim's browser resolves them before the request reaches the cache
Otherwise the origin always returns a 500 error
Encoded dot-segments are the only form caches recognize as static
Browsers refuse to send any URL containing a dot
questions.explain: If dot-segments are left unencoded, the victim's browser resolves them before the request is sent, so they never reach the cache. Encoding them preserves the traversal for the cache/origin to (dis)agree on.

questions.q: When detecting whether the origin normalizes paths, why use a non-idempotent method like POST?
choices: It uses a non-cacheable resource, so results reflect the origin's behavior rather than the cache's
POST requests are always faster than GET
Only POST requests can contain a traversal sequence
The cache always caches POST responses
questions.explain: A POST (non-idempotent) request targets a non-cacheable resource, so the response reveals how the origin handles the traversal (e.g. /aaa/..%2fprofile) without the cache interfering.

questions.q: To exploit origin normalization (origin resolves the path, cache does not), what payload structure is used?
choices: /<static-directory-prefix>/..%2f<dynamic-path>, e.g. /assets/..%2fprofile
/<dynamic-path>%2f%2e%2e%2f<static-prefix>
/<dynamic-path>;<static-prefix>.css
/<static-prefix>/<dynamic-path> with no traversal
questions.explain: Use /<static-directory-prefix>/..%2f<dynamic-path> (e.g. /assets/..%2fprofile). The cache sees the /assets prefix and caches it; the origin decodes and resolves the traversal to /profile.

questions.q: When exploiting cache normalization (cache resolves the path, origin does not), why must you add a delimiter after the dynamic path, as in /profile;%2f%2e%2e%2fstatic?
choices: Traversal alone makes the origin see a path that errors; a delimiter the origin uses but the cache doesn't lets the origin truncate to the dynamic data while the cache resolves to /static
The delimiter encrypts the traversal so the cache ignores it
Without a delimiter the browser refuses the request
The delimiter forces the origin to cache the response itself
questions.explain: With /profile%2f%2e%2e%2fstatic alone the origin sees that literal path and errors. Adding a delimiter it uses but the cache doesn't (e.g. ;) lets the origin truncate to /profile while the cache resolves the traversal to /static and caches it.

questions.q: File name cache rules (e.g. for robots.txt, index.html, favicon.ico) match the path how?
choices: By an exact file name match
By a path prefix
By any file sharing the same extension
By the response's content length
questions.explain: File name rules use an exact file name match for files that rarely change (robots.txt, index.html, favicon.ico).

questions.q: Because file name rules use an exact match, which WCD case is the only one that works against them?
choices: The cache-resolves / origin-doesn't case, using the file name in place of the directory prefix
The origin-resolves / cache-doesn't case
The path-mapping case with an added extension
Any case, since exact matches are the easiest to exploit
questions.explain: An exact file name match means only the cache-normalization method works: e.g. /<dynamic-path><delimiter>%2f%2e%2e%2findex.html, where the cache resolves to /index.html and the origin returns the dynamic data.

questions.q: Which Cache-Control directive(s) should be set on dynamic resources to help prevent WCD?
choices: no-store, private
public, max-age=31536000
must-revalidate only
immutable, public
questions.explain: Marking dynamic resources Cache-Control: no-store, private tells caches not to store them. The CDN must also be configured so its rules don't override Cache-Control.

questions.q: What does a CDN WCD protection like Cloudflare's Cache Deception Armor do?
choices: Checks that the response Content-Type matches the URL's file extension before caching
Blocks every request that contains a dot-segment
Encrypts all cached responses at rest
Disables caching entirely for the whole site
questions.explain: Cache Deception Armor verifies that the response Content-Type matches the file extension in the URL, so a dynamic HTML response disguised with a .css path is not cached.

questions.q: Which of the following are recommended measures to prevent web cache deception?
choices: Mark dynamic resources with Cache-Control: no-store, private
Configure the CDN so its caching rules don't override Cache-Control
Verify there are no discrepancies between how the origin and cache interpret URL paths
Serve all sensitive pages only over plain HTTP
questions.explain: Prevention includes setting no-store/private on dynamic content, stopping the CDN from overriding Cache-Control, enabling CDN WCD protections, and ensuring origin and cache interpret paths identically. Serving over plain HTTP is not a defense.
